strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: existing RVOS benchmarks (A2D-Sentences, Ref-YouTube-VOS, MeViS) are limited to clips of a few seconds, while real-world videos are minutes long. Long-RVOS (2,193 videos, 60.3s average, 36.7h total, 2.1M masks) is by a large margin the longest and largest RVOS resource, and Table 1 makes the scale advantage clear.

The dataset construction is thorough and credible: multi-source collection (TAO, VidOR, Ego-Exo4D) with explicit selection criteria, three description types (static/dynamic/hybrid) enabling fine-grained diagnosis, human text annotation with expert validation rather than automatic scaling tricks, and an iterative check-correct workflow for the SAM2-generated masks.

The newly introduced tIoU and vIoU metrics are well motivated: the paper convincingly argues that per-frame J&F cannot capture the ability to predict object absence, and the benchmark results (e.g., SAM2-based methods performing poorly despite SOTA on short benchmarks) validate the benchmark's diagnostic value.

The empirical analysis is informative beyond leaderboard numbers: the oracle analysis with SAM2 (52.8-54.5 J&F on Long-RVOS vs. 77.3-80.6 on MeViS) quantifies the long-video difficulty independently of language grounding; the fine-grained results reveal a systematic static-attribute bias in current models; and the consistent tIoU across models exposes a shared temporal-consistency weakness.

ReferMo is a sensible, simple baseline: clip decomposition with keyframe + MPEG-4 motion vectors, gated image-motion fusion, and global inter-clip interaction yields a solid improvement (51.3/71.2/42.6 vs. next best 48.7/71.7/41.2 overall) at high FPS (52.5), and ablations support each design choice (motion info contributes +1.6-2.1% J&F).
weaknesses: Mask ground truth is produced by SAM2 from bounding-box prompts. Although the check-correct loop mitigates this, a substantial portion of the 'ground truth' is model-generated, which introduces circularity: the benchmark's top method also uses SAM2 for propagation at inference, so evaluation may partially favor SAM2-compatible pipelines and inherit SAM2's systematic errors as label noise.

The tIoU/vIoU metrics are borrowed from spatiotemporal video grounding ([40, 52]); the paper cites this inspiration, but the framing as 'we introduce two new metrics' overstates novelty. More importantly, no analysis of metric failure modes (e.g., sensitivity to sparse predictions, behavior with multiple referring instances) is provided.

ReferMo's evaluation on Long-RVOS only raises a generalization concern: all competitors are trained on Long-RVOS from scratch, and there is no zero-shot or cross-dataset evaluation (e.g., ReferMo on MeViS/Ref-YouTube-VOS, or existing models fine-tuned on short data then tested on Long-RVOS) to show how the benchmark relates to prior distributions.

The baseline itself is heavily dependent on SAM2 for non-keyframe masks, which weakens the claim of better 'language-guided understanding' — the tIoU deficit relative to ReferDINO (71.2 vs. 71.7) is acknowledged but under-analyzed, and the keyframe-only improvement over ReferDINO is small (+0.5% J&F, within plausible run-to-run variance without significance testing).

Some scope limitations are under-discussed: 71.9% of objects are humans (bias inherited from source datasets), the test set is only 225 videos / 2,588 sentences, and legal/redistribution considerations for masks derived from TAO/VidOR/Ego-Exo4D are not addressed. The 'Project Page:' field in the title block is empty, and no explicit statement of code/dataset release is given, hurting reproducibility as presented.

Presentation is generally clear but has minor issues: Section 5.1 says 'three types of descriptions: static, temporal and hybrid' (should be 'dynamic'), Table 3(b) keyframe ablation is brief, and the claim that ReferMo 'significantly outperforms other models across various types and metrics' should be tempered given the tIoU exception and the modest margins on some entries.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: existing RVOS benchmarks (A2D-Sentences, Ref-YouTube-VOS, MeViS) are limited to clips of a few seconds, and Long-RVOS is a credible first attempt at a minute-level RVOS benchmark with 2,193 videos averaging 60.3s, 36.7 total hours, 2.1M masks, and 163 object classes (Table 1, Figure 4).

The dataset construction pipeline is described in reasonable detail, including selection criteria (Section 3.1), a three-type description taxonomy (static/dynamic/hybrid) with balanced distribution (Figure 4f), expert quality validation of text, and an iterative check-correct workflow for mask refinement, which speaks to annotation effort and quality control.
The oracle analysis with SAM2 (Table 3a: 52.8–54.5 J&F on Long-RVOS vs. 77.3–80.6 on MeViS) is a useful diagnostic that quantifies the long-term challenge independent of any referring model.

Benchmarking six recent methods under consistent training settings, and including FPS, gives the community an actionable baseline comparison and a clear negative finding (SAM2-based methods degrade on long videos).

The ReferMo design is sensible for the compute constraint: keyframe-only supervision with MPEG-4 motion vectors and SAM2 propagation at inference achieves the best FPS (52.5) alongside the best overall accuracy.
weaknesses: Ground-truth masks are largely produced by SAM2 propagation from sparse boxes rather than fully manual annotation. This creates a circularity risk: the evaluation rewards SAM2-style tracking behavior, and two of the baselines (SAMWISE, GLUS) explicitly build on SAM2. The paper does not quantify inter-annotator agreement or report a human-verified mask subset to validate that the pseudo-labels are reliable ground truth.

The claimed novelty of 'two new metrics' is overstated: tIoU and vIoU are directly adapted from spatio-temporal video grounding ([40, 52], acknowledged in Section 3.4). More importantly, Table 2 shows tIoU is nearly non-discriminative across all methods (68.0–71.9, a ~4-point spread despite large differences in J&F), which undermines the paper's argument that this metric meaningfully captures a capability current models lack. The paper notes this but does not analyze why the metric saturates or what an empty-mask prediction baseline (e.g., always-empty or GT-presence-prior) would score.

ReferMo's improvement, while consistent, is modest in absolute terms (51.3 vs. 48.7 J&F over ReferDINO) and is architecturally incremental: it combines MPEG-4 tokenization from Video-LaVIT [18], dual cross-attention from GroundingDINO [28], and Hungarian-based temporal alignment from ReferDINO [25]. The claimed 0.5% keyframe J&F gain over ReferDINO (Table 3b) is within typical variance and no significance analysis or multiple runs are reported.

Generalization is not evaluated: all models are trained on Long-RVOS, and there is no cross-dataset experiment (e.g., training on MeViS and testing on Long-RVOS, or fine-tuning effects) to show the benchmark transfers or that improvements are not dataset-specific overfitting to the SAM2-generated mask distribution.

The benchmark is compiled from pre-existing datasets (TAO, VidOR, Ego-Exo4D, and their federated sources). The paper does not discuss licensing/redistribution constraints for releasing re-annotated subsets of these sources, nor annotator compensation details—relevant for a dataset contribution.

Several evaluation details are under-specified or missing: how shot changes interact with SAM2 clip segmentation, how tIoU/vIoU treat multiple-instance videos, error bars/confidence intervals on the 225-video test set, and qualitative results showing failure modes. The 'Project Page' placeholder on page 1 is empty, limiting reproducibility assessment at review time.

Some claims are weaker than stated: 'fine-grained evaluation' conclusions (dynamic type is harder) are supported only by aggregate score deltas, and the explanation for ReferMo's slightly lower tIoU vs. ReferDINO is speculative ('we speculate') without supporting analysis.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated gap: existing RVOS benchmarks (A2D-Sentences, Ref-YouTube-VOS, MeViS) are limited to clips of a few seconds, and the paper convincingly argues this hides real weaknesses of current models. The new benchmark (2,193 videos, 60.3s average duration, 36.7 total hours, 163 object classes, 24,689 descriptions) is substantially larger and longer than prior RVOS datasets (Table 1, Figure 1).

Thoughtful dataset construction: multi-source curation (TAO, VidOR, Ego-Exo4D) with explicit selection criteria, three description types (static/dynamic/hybrid) with balanced distribution (Figure 4f), and a documented iterative check–correct annotation workflow rather than purely automatic mask propagation, which increases confidence in annotation quality.

The introduction of tIoU and vIoU addresses a genuine evaluation deficiency: frame-wise J&F cannot capture temporal consistency or correct prediction of object absence. Eq. (1)-(2) are simple, well-defined, and the metric analysis (Table 2) yields an interesting finding: models with very different J&F have similar tIoU, suggesting temporal identification, not mask quality, is the bottleneck.

The benchmarking of 6 SOTA methods under consistent settings, plus the SAM2 oracle analysis (Table 3a, ~25% gap vs. MeViS), provides strong evidence that long-form RVOS is genuinely unsolved rather than merely a scale issue. The observation that SAM2-based methods (VideoLISA, SAMWISE, GLUS) underperform on long videos despite SOTA short-video results is a valuable insight.

ReferMo is technically reasonable and well-explained: MPEG-4 motion vectors are a cheap, scalable way to expand temporal receptive field, the sparse keyframe-only supervision is sensible, and ablations (Table 3b,c) support each design choice (motion contributes +1.6% J&F with one frame). The method achieves the best overall results (51.3 J&F, 42.6 vIoU) with favorable FPS (52.5).
Writing is generally clear and well-organized; the paper is self-contained and the experimental setup (splits, hyperparameters, compute) is reported in enough detail to be reproducible in principle.
weaknesses: Mask annotations are SAM2-propagated from sparse bounding boxes with human correction. The paper does not quantify residual annotation noise (e.g., human-agreement IoU on a sample, or disagreement rate between check-correct rounds). Since the oracle SAM2 upper bound is only ~53 J&F, some of the 'long-term difficulty' may conflate model limitation with annotation ambiguity or hard tracking cases.

The claimed novelty of tIoU/vIoU is overstated: the paper itself admits these are 'inspired by the field of spatiotemporal video grounding [40, 52]'. They are adapted, not new; the text should be more precise about what is genuinely novel (the adoption in RVOS evaluation, not the metrics themselves).

ReferMo is largely an engineering combination of existing components (ReferDINO's architecture and Hungarian alignment, MPEG-4 motion vectors following Video-LaVIT, SAM2 for propagation, dual cross-attention from GroundingDINO). The ablation shows the gains over ReferDINO on keyframes are modest (49.6 vs. 49.1 J&F, i.e., 0.5%), and ReferMo is actually slightly worse than ReferDINO on tIoU (71.2 vs. 71.7). The headline improvements on Table 2 should be interpreted with this in mind; no statistical significance or variance over seeds is reported.

Potential unfairness in the comparison: the authors note existing methods sample only 4-8 frames per video in training due to GPU limits while ReferMo samples 6 clips. It is unclear whether SAM2-based competitors were given comparable tuning effort or frame budgets; the claim that their weakness stems from 'tracking rather than language understanding' could partly reflect suboptimal adaptation to long videos rather than a fundamental limitation.

No cross-dataset/zero-shot experiments: all models are trained on Long-RVOS. Showing how models trained on MeViS/Ref-YouTube-VOS transfer to Long-RVOS (and vice versa) would strengthen the claim that the benchmark measures a new capability rather than a distribution shift.

Missing details reduce reproducibility and completeness: the 'Project Page' on page 1 is empty (no URL or release commitment stated in the main text), the dataset split rationale is not described (are splits stratified by source dataset or description type?), licensing/redistribution rights for videos from TAO/VidOR/Ego-Exo4D are not discussed, and the motion-vector extraction details are deferred to a supplementary that was not provided for review.

Some statistics raise questions the paper does not address: object duration averages 47.8s while video duration averages 60.3s, meaning objects are visible in ~79% of frames on average — the 'long-term' challenge regarding absence may be less severe than the framing suggests; a breakdown of the fraction of frames where the target is absent would clarify this.

Minor presentation issues: inconsistent terminology ('static, temporal and hybrid' on p.8 vs. 'static, dynamic and hybrid' elsewhere), typos ('embeded', 'remain focus on', 'resort the dimension'), and Figure 6 in the main text has some cramped labels.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and clearly articulated gap: existing RVOS benchmarks (A2D-Sentences, Ref-YouTube-VOS, MeViS) use clips of only a few seconds, while Long-RVOS provides 2,193 videos averaging 60.3s with 2.1M masks, 6,703 objects, and 163 object classes (Table 1), making it the first large-scale, minute-level RVOS benchmark.

The dataset construction is well documented and careful: multi-source collection (TAO, VidOR, Ego-Exo4D) with explicit selection criteria, three description types (Static/Dynamic/Hybrid) with a balanced distribution (Table 2), a validation team enforcing a distinguishability principle, no artificial text augmentation, and a SAM2-based iterative check–correct loop for mask quality. Supplementary Tables 7–8 quantitatively demonstrate harder long-video attributes (e.g., 36.2% full occlusion and 11.5% long-term reappearance vs. 15.1%/0.1% in MeViS).

The two new metrics (tIoU and vIoU) are well motivated and the analysis supports their value: Table 3 shows J&F varies widely while tIoU stays relatively stable across methods, indicating that frame-averaged metrics may have overestimated temporal robustness of current models.

The benchmarking is broad (7 SOTA methods across SAM2-based and non-SAM2-based families) and the oracle analysis (Table 4a: SAM2 with GT prompts reaches only 54–57 J&F on Long-RVOS vs. 77–81 on MeViS) convincingly establishes the dataset's long-term difficulty rather than attributing low scores purely to model weaknesses.

ReferMo is a sensible and effective baseline: MPEG-4 motion vectors are cheap to extract (748 FPS, supplementary), keyframe-only supervision reduces training cost, and ablations (Tables 4b, 5, 10) cleanly decompose gains from keyframe decomposition (+1.1), motion features (+1.1), and gating mechanisms (+1.1 over naive fusion). Robustness under increasing occlusion rates (Table 6) is a valuable stress test.

Strong and consistent empirical results: ReferMo outperforms all 7 baselines across description types, metrics, description lengths (Table 11), event complexity (Table 12), and occlusion brackets, at competitive speed (52.5 FPS vs. 3.6–8.7 for SAM2-based competitors).
weaknesses: The methodological novelty of ReferMo is limited. The core components — Swin-Tiny backbone, dual cross-attention fusion, Hungarian-matching object alignment, and the object-consistent temporal enhancer — are explicitly adopted from ReferDINO (supplementary Sec. 8). The genuinely new elements (keyframe-plus-motion-vector decomposition, gating-based image-motion fusion) are modest architectural additions, so the paper's value rests primarily on the benchmark.

The mask annotations are produced by SAM2 propagation from sparse bounding-box prompts and then corrected by annotators; the paper does not report any quantitative annotation quality control for masks (e.g., sampled re-annotation agreement or error rates after the check–correct loop), only for text. Given 2.1M masks, unquantified residual SAM2 propagation error is a material concern for a benchmark intended as ground truth.

No inter-annotator agreement or consistency statistics are reported for the 30K text descriptions collected from 20 college students; the distinction between Static/Dynamic/Hybrid types relies on subjective annotator judgment, and quality verification is described only as removal of violating descriptions.

All benchmarked models are trained solely on Long-RVOS without external data; while this is fair within the paper, several methods (especially MLLM-based ones like VideoLISA, GLUS) are presumably designed for multi-source training, and the strong observed degradations may partly reflect training-protocol mismatch rather than intrinsic inability to handle long videos.

The proposed metrics are closely related to existing spatio-temporal video grounding metrics (the authors cite [42, 56] themselves), so 'two new metrics' overstates the novelty; they are adapted rather than invented. Also, tIoU/vIoU treat non-empty mask prediction as the temporal signal, but different baselines may have very different tendencies to output empty masks, and the paper does not discuss how this asymmetry affects cross-method fairness.

Benchmark results rely heavily on SAM2 propagation at inference (keyframe predictions as anchors); Table 4c shows SAM2 contributes 2.5–2.7 J&F over alternatives, and the headline gains over SAM2-based competitors partly conflate the tracker's quality with the referring/grounding component. The occlusion-bracket analysis (Table 6) partially addresses this but the confound is not fully disentangled.

Minor presentation issues: several typos ('Cuite' for Cutie, 'soly', 'revist', 'revisit' needed in Fig. 8 comparisons only against one baseline), the description-type label is inconsistently written as 'Temporal' in Sec. 5.1 vs. 'Dynamic' elsewhere, and the text annotation pipeline's licensing/redistribution conditions for the federated TAO sources are not discussed.

The dataset is heavily human-centric (71.9% of objects), which limits the diversity claim relative to the framing, and the benchmark currently excludes stuff classes — acknowledged by the authors as a limitation.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: existing RVOS benchmarks (A2D-Sentences, Ref-Youtube-VOS, MeViS) contain clips of only a few seconds, and Long-RVOS provides the first minute-level (60.3s average) RVOS benchmark at meaningful scale (2,193 videos, 2.1M masks, 24,689 descriptions), as substantiated in Table 1.

The dataset construction is careful and transparent: explicit selection criteria (Sec. 3.1), a structured text annotation protocol with three description types and a dedicated validation team, and an iterative check–correct workflow with an interactive SAM2-based tool for mask refinement (Sec. 3.2).

The benchmarking effort is substantial: 7 recent methods (including SAM2-based ones like SAMWISE and GLUS) are retrained under a controlled protocol (trained solely on Long-RVOS), and the results (Table 3) yield a meaningful finding that SAM2-based SOTA methods degrade severely on long videos, suggesting their gains come from tracking rather than language understanding.

The evaluation is reasonably thorough for the baseline: oracle analysis with SAM2 prompts (Table 4a, ~25% gap vs. MeViS), ablations of video decomposition, motion fusion, mask-propagation backends (XMem++, Cutie), occlusion-rate stratification (Table 6), plus supplementary analyses on description length, event complexity, and gating mechanisms (Tables 10–12).

The proposed ReferMo is simple, data-efficient (24h on 8 A6000s), and fast (52.5 FPS), and consistently outperforms competitors across description types, occlusion brackets, and description lengths, supporting the claim that it is a useful foundation for long-video RVOS.
weaknesses: The claimed metric contribution is overstated. tIoU and vIoU are directly adapted from spatio-temporal video grounding [42, 56], as the authors themselves acknowledge ('Inspired by the field of spatiotemporal video grounding'). Moreover, tIoU is nearly saturated across all methods (59.2–74.2 in Table 3), limiting its discriminative power; the genuinely informative new signal is mostly the low vIoU values.

The absolute improvement of ReferMo over the strongest baseline (ReferDINO) is modest: +4.5 J&F / +1.7 tIoU / +1.3 vIoU overall (Table 3), with gains in tIoU and vIoU being marginal. The ablations show the architectural novelty contributes small increments (keyframe decomposition +1.1, motion +1.1 J&F in Table 4b), so the method contribution is closer to an engineering adaptation of ReferDINO than a new technique.

Reproducibility is not demonstrated: the 'Project Page' field on page 1 is blank, and there is no explicit statement that the dataset, annotation platform, or code will be released. For a benchmark paper, public release is essential to the claimed contribution, and its absence materially weakens the paper.

The benchmark is built by redistributing/re-annotating videos from TAO (itself federated across Charades, LaSOT, AVA, YFCC100M, etc.), VidOR, and Ego-Exo4D; the paper does not discuss licensing or terms-of-use implications of republishing these sources with new annotations.

Mask quality depends on SAM2 propagation plus human correction, but no quantitative annotation-quality audit (e.g., double-annotation IoU agreement, inter-annotator consistency of the text descriptions' distinguishability criterion) is reported, which is standard for dataset papers claiming 'high-quality' annotations.

The comparison protocol, while controlled, trains all methods only on Long-RVOS; several compared methods (e.g., VideoLISA, GLUS) are designed for much broader training mixtures, so their very low scores (e.g., VideoLISA at 14.0 J&F) partly reflect out-of-distribution training regimes rather than long-video capability alone, which complicates the interpretation in the 'Overall Comparison' discussion.

Presentation has notable sloppiness for a submission at this level: e.g., 'soly' (p.8), 'revisit' misspelled as 'revist' (supp.), 'embeded' (p.6), Section 5.1 inconsistently calling the description types 'Static, Temporal and Hybrid' when the taxonomy is Static/Dynamic/Hybrid, and reference [44] (CondConv/conditional convolutions) cited for a 'projection loss' without clear connection.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and clearly motivated gap: existing RVOS benchmarks (A2D-Sentences, Ref-YouTube-VOS, MeViS) are limited to clips of a few seconds, while Long-RVOS provides 2,193 videos averaging 60.3s with 2.1M masks and 24,689 human-written descriptions, making it the first large-scale, minute-level RVOS benchmark (Table 1).

The dataset construction is thorough and well-documented: multi-source video collection (TAO, VidOR, Ego-Exo4D) with explicit selection criteria, three description types (Static/Dynamic/Hybrid) with balanced distribution (Table 2), a validation team quality check for text, and an iterative check-correct loop with SAM2-assisted interactive tooling for masks. Supplementary Tables 7-8 quantify long-video attributes (occlusion, disappearance-reappearance, view change) relative to MeViS.

The new evaluation metrics (tIoU, vIoU) are well-motivated and technically sound: they reward correct prediction of object absence via empty masks, which frame-averaged J&F cannot capture. The empirical observation that tIoU is stable while J&F varies widely across methods (Sec. 5.2) supports the claim that prior metrics conflate spatial quality with temporal consistency.

The benchmarking of 7 SOTA methods is comprehensive, with consistent results on both validation (Table 9) and test (Table 3) sets, plus fine-grained breakdowns by description type, occlusion rate (Table 6), description length (Table 11), and event complexity (Table 12). The finding that SAM2-based methods degrade sharply on long videos, while performing well on short benchmarks, is an interesting and useful insight for the community.

ReferMo is a sensible, well-executed baseline: keyframe+motion-vector decomposition (MPEG-4 motion vectors are efficient, 748 FPS extraction), gated image-motion fusion, and local-to-global interaction. Ablations (Tables 4b, 5, 10) isolate the contribution of each component, and the oracle analysis (Table 4a, ~25% gap vs. MeViS) quantifies the difficulty of the new benchmark.

The paper is generally clearly written, with reasonable reproducibility signals: implementation details (backbone, SAM2 version, clip sampling, 24h on 8 A6000s), a public project page, and a limitations section.
weaknesses: Annotation reliability of the masks is a concern: masks are generated by SAM2 propagation from sparse bounding boxes and then corrected by annotators; the paper does not report any quantitative annotation quality assessment (e.g., human-vs-human consistency, IoU between annotator and final mask on a sampled subset, or inter-annotator agreement for description validity). For a benchmark paper whose central artifact is the dataset, such validation statistics would materially strengthen the contribution.

The fairness of the comparison in Table 3 is partially compromised: all baselines are retrained solely on Long-RVOS, but they were designed under different training regimes (frame sampling rates, data scale expectations). Some baselines (e.g., MLLM-based VideoLISA, GLUS, RGA3) may be severely under-trained in this setting, so the magnitude of their degradation could partly reflect adaptation cost rather than a fundamental inability to handle long videos. The claim that SAM2-based methods' short-video gains stem 'primarily from SAM2's tracking rather than language understanding' is plausible but not directly evidenced.

ReferMo depends on SAM2 for mask propagation on non-keyframes, and the benchmark metrics evaluate the full mask sequence; thus part of ReferMo's advantage over non-SAM2 baselines may come from the tracker rather than from better language-object reasoning. Table 4c partially addresses this (XMem++/Cutie variants still beat SAM2-based competitors), which is appreciated, but the decomposition of ReferMo's gains into reasoning vs. tracking is not fully quantified.

The tIoU/vIoU metrics are close adaptations of existing spatiotemporal video grounding metrics (the paper itself cites [42, 56]); the novelty of the metrics is modest, and edge cases (e.g., how predictions on frames where the object is absent affect J&F averaging, and whether tIoU rewards trivially predicting empty masks on hard videos) are not analyzed.

Motion vectors at macroblock resolution (H/16 x W/16) are coarse and only approximate; the paper claims they capture short-term motion adequately, but there is no comparison against denser motion representations (e.g., optical flow) to validate this design choice.

Legal/ethical aspects of redistribution are not discussed: Long-RVOS is built from TAO, VidOR, Ego-Exo4D (and TAO's federated sources including LaSOT, BDD-100K, etc.). The paper does not state whether source videos will actually be redistributed or only provided via the original datasets, nor does it discuss annotator compensation or consent for the annotation platform.

Several aspects are deferred to the supplementary or left vague: the keyframe/clip decomposition details, the SAM2 prompt mechanism at inference, and the exact test-set release protocol (whether ground truth of the test split will be withheld for a leaderboard) are not fully specified in the main paper.

Minor presentation issues: typos ('soly', 'Cuite' for Cutie, 'revist', 'embeded'), 'Static, Temporal and Hybrid' in Sec 5.1 inconsistent with 'Dynamic' used elsewhere, and Figure 1's y-axis (Total Hours) makes the MeViS bubble placement visually ambiguous.
